articles.title: Video Game Workers at Blizzard Won First Union Contracts
articles.author: Dan DiMaggio
articles.content_excerpt: Workers who make some of the world’s most popular video games, including World of Warcraft and Diablo , won their first union contracts in early September, in an important step forward for organizing in the tech industry. The 1,900 workers are employed by Blizzard, which was acquired by Microsoft in 2023 in the largest deal ever in the video game industry. Their new Communications Workers (CWA) contracts include recall rights and guaranteed severance packages for laid-off workers — significant wins, since tech and video game workers have seen waves of layoffs in the last few years. Workers on various Activision Blizzard teams have voted to join CWA since 2022. articles.title: According to Polls, Americans Like Socialism a Lot
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: Socialism is more popular than it’s been for a long time, both socialism and its most well-known adherents appeal to a surprisingly diverse voter base, and most people still have no idea who Hasan Piker is. Those are just a few of the takeaways from a crop of polls conducted over the past month or so, which together suggest the radicalized, antiestablishment zeal that’s taken over the Democratic electorate and opened the door for a rising socialist insurgency is still going strong, with a few surprises in tow. And they come at a potentially crucial time, as socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez weighs whether to make a run for president in 2028, a campaign that many socialists view as pivotal to the future prospects of their movement as a whole. articles.title: Literacy Is Another Casualty of the Decline of Democracy
articles.author: John Livesey
articles.content_excerpt: Approximately two years ago, a bizarre new genre of AI-generated content began to emerge online. Suddenly social media was filled with short-form videos depicting hypersexual anthropomorphic fruit, embroiled in increasingly far-fetched and soapy plot lines. In one video, a voluptuous strawberry cheats on her watermelon husband, and gives birth to two wolf cubs. In another, an emasculated orange takes revenge on a womanizing banana who has stolen his girlfriend. In a particularly violent iteration, a young tangerine is bullied by his homophobic father and ends up juicing his whole family. It is easy to dismiss these shlocky and incoherent narratives as mere “AI slop.” But they are also endemic to a broader culture. articles.title: The San Jose Execution
articles.author: Silicon Valley DSA
articles.content_excerpt: This statement was written by members of the Silicon Valley DSA Liberation and Justice Working Group . A Tragedy of Systemic Violence The events that unfolded on January 21st, 2026, in San Jose, California, serve as a chilling, visceral testament to the enduring crisis of systemic violence against Black lives in America. Mohamed Husein was a son, a brother, and a father murdered in cold blood for fleeing from San Jose Police Department officers to avoid arrest for a crime spree. He was literally running for his life, attempting to escape a system that, for far too many, equates criminality with a death sentence. articles.title: Greece’s Neo-Nazis Are Back
articles.author: Georgios Samaras
articles.content_excerpt: For over seven years after it entered parliament in May 2012, Golden Dawn was at the heart of Greece’s political life. Its rise was accompanied by scenes that should have made its character unmistakable. During the June 2012 election campaign, MP Ilias Kasidiaris assaulted two female left-wing politicians live on TV, while numerous other key members were documented openly expressing admiration for Adolf Hitler . Beyond parliament, something far darker was taking place. Golden Dawn was not simply an extremist political party but, a Greek court would later establish, a criminal organization orchestrating a web of violence. articles.title: What The Flock: Prison Populists and Palantyranny
articles.author: Pine and Roses -- Maine DSA
articles.content_excerpt: There is a peculiar American humiliation in having to explain why you would like to buy groceries without helping populate a police database. You needed eggs. Apparently, you also owed somebody a record of the trip. Flock Safety’s roadside cameras collect license plates, vehicle characteristics, locations, and timestamps. Pass one and your car can become a searchable observation, available to an investigator with access. The company describes these as snapshots of public vehicle information . Such a modest word, snapshot. A birthday. A beach. Your car passing an intersection while you are trying to get through a Tuesday. A collection of those observations has a different character. articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s Yemen Strategy Has Fallen to Pieces
articles.author: Helen Lackner
articles.content_excerpt: Over the past few weeks, Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Huthis, has launched an offensive and made big territorial gains. The latest turn in the Yemeni civil war could have major implications for the world economy, as it involves one of its most important trade routes through the Red Sea. It certainly poses a big challenge for Yemen’s neighbor Saudi Arabia. Helen Lackner is a leading expert on the politics of Yemen and the author of several books about the country. She spoke to Jacobin about the background to the latest developments and what is likely to happen next. This is an edited transcript from Jacobin’s Long Reads podcast. articles.title: Greed and Economic Desperation Are Fueling Sudan’s Civil War
articles.author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
articles.content_excerpt: I used to pass the biscuit factory in Soba without going in. People I knew went in for a twelve-hour shift on a line that smelled of sugar and oil. In 2021, the number that stuck was 1,500 pounds for the shift. In Haj Yousif, where Iqbal lived, the rent for a single room was 30,000 pounds a month. You had to work twenty factory days just to cover rent. Meanwhile, the Rapid Support Forces were offering people 15,000 a day, a uniform, and a phone. Those three numbers explain more about Sudan’s war than any map I have been shown since. What happened in Sudan was not primarily a story of people choosing violence.
